Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Known People: Related people, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Sameer was twenty-nine when his then-partner, a distant cousin who had moved in with him, began a pattern of escalating physical control. The violence never followed a predictable rhythm; it arrived with the sudden weight of his cousin’s hands, the sharp pressure against his left shoulder and the ball of his right foot, and a terrifying proximity that left Sameer unable to speak or move. When the abuse finally crossed a line, Sameer called for help, and that night brought uniformed officers to his apartment. The combination of his cousin’s presence, the thick smell of stale sweat clinging to his work shirt, and the commanding voices of the police officers became locked together in Sameer’s nervous system. In the years that followed, he never found a way to translate those nights into language. When his wife gently asked what had happened, he could not shape the experience into sentences; the memory refused to take the form of words, leaving only a hollow pressure in his chest and the quiet certainty that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. The symptoms settled into his daily rhythm as overlapping realities. He stopped exercising because the physical exertion left him breathing heavily, and the dampness of his own skin reminded him too much of the air in that apartment. He kept his work shirts buried in the back of his closet, avoiding anything that felt too close to the heavy cotton his ex-partner had worn. Social invitations piled up unanswered; he turned them down because he was certain that known faces, especially relatives or family friends, might bring the same unpredictable weight into the room. At home, he had come to believe that true rest required him to stay alert, propping himself against the headboard with his back straight, listening for any shift in the house. He only felt secure inside his study, a narrow space where the door stayed shut and the windows faced away from the street. When the memory returned, it did not arrive as a story but as a sudden, sharp ache in the exact spots where he had been pinned, and in those moments he was certain the floor was tilting again, making it feel as though the abuse were unfolding in real time. These habits intersected sharply with his life as a military medic. The base clinic, with its fluorescent lighting and steady cadence of commands, became a place where he braced himself for sudden noise. A dropped stethoscope or a crashing tray of instruments sent his shoulders hiking up before his brain could register the harmless cause, his body flinching with a readiness for impact that left him exhausted by mid-afternoon. During a busy shift, a patient leaning over his examination table exhaled a thick, metallic scent of exertion, and Sameer had to step back, his chest tightening until the smell faded. He began to sit at the edges of team briefings, avoiding peer conversations and limiting his interactions to strictly necessary clinical tasks. The authority of his medic role, once a source of steady pride, now felt like a uniform that drew unwanted attention and highlighted his own perceived failures. He had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, a flaw that had made him unable to prevent the abuse or protect himself afterward, a reality that sat heavy alongside the quiet fact that the people responsible had faced no consequences. Now, at forty-nine, Sameer sits in his car outside the VA mental health clinic, the engine off. His wife has told him that the distance between them has grown into a wall he no longer knows how to climb down, and he has realized he can no longer manage the silence in his study alone. He came to this intake because the waiting has become too exhausting, and because he is tired of his body reacting to ordinary sounds as though danger were imminent. He does not know if therapy will help, but he is most afraid that the physical pain in his shoulder and foot will continue to echo without explanation, and he hopes, however faintly, to finally lay the weight down without having to carry it in isolation.
